# Exact nonsimplex prisms and cones with oblique centroidal sections

These constructions generate exact stationary sections for falsifying
candidate inequalities. They do not prove the general scalar-centroid
correction or the general weighted-section inequality.

For a convex body K containing0 and a central oriented plane with
centroidal section, let p be its cap fraction and
s=S(u·g_K)/|K|, with unit inward normal u and section area S. A scalar
correction c≥0 would require p−γ_d≥cs. Its exact feasibility interval
is obtained by intersecting these one-dimensional inequalities.

## 1. A prism construction with independently nonsymmetric exterior mass

Fix rational1<h<2 and

    a=2(h²−h+1)/(3(h−1)).

Then a>h. Let

    W={(x,y):x≤1, |y|≤a+x},
    D=W∩{x≥−h}.

The width of D at x is2(a+x). Its y centroid is0 by reflection and

    ∫_{−h}^1 x·2(a+x)dx
      =2(1+h³)/3+a(1−h²)=0

by the displayed choice of a. Thus D has centroid0. Choose any
rational polygon B with D⊂B⊂W, whose extra vertices have x<−h.
For example B may be the convex hull of D and an arbitrary point
(−ℓ,b), h<ℓ<a, |b|<a−ℓ. This is generally a nonsymmetric pentagon.
Then B∩{|x|≤h}=D because h>1.

Take K=B×[−1,1]. Its centroid is(g_B,0) and volume2|B|. Both central
planes z=±x/h have centroidal sections: their sections are the graphs
of these linear functions over D, so their area measures differ from
planar area by a constant factor. Orient the caps as
z≥x/h and−z≥x/h. Since points of B outside D have x<−h, they are
fully captured; inside D the captured interval fraction is
(1−x/h)/2. The centroid identity for D yields

    p=1−|D|/(2|B|),
    s=−|D|(g_B)_x/(2h|B|).                           (1)

Their complementary cuts have data(1−p,−s). Here
|D|=(a+1)²−(a−h)².

A vertical central plane over a planar chord of B with midpoint0 is
also centroidal: its section is the product of that centered chord
with[−1,1]. Its p and s are exactly the corresponding planar p and s
for B. For a rational polygon every transverse intersection of an
edge of B with an edge of−B is a rational point q with±q on∂B;
these are exact centered chord endpoints. With raw normal Rq, its
normalized coarea vector is2Rq/|B|. Thus all quantities in(1) and in
these vertical constraints are rational and directly checkable.

## 2. Projective polygons give a nonsymmetric cone construction

Let D⊂R² be any rational polygon with centroid0. Choose rational
k∈R² satisfying

    −1/2<k·x<1           for every x∈D,

and set B=T_{−k}(D), so B's vertices are x/(1−k·x). Let

    K=conv(B×{−1},(0,0,2)).

The body has volume|B| and centroid

    g_K=((3/4)g_B,−1/4).

The central plane z=3k·x meets each apex-to-base segment at

    x=(2/3)T_k(b),      z=3k·x.

The intersection parameter is2(1−k·x_D)/3∈(0,1) by the parameter
bounds. Its section is therefore exactly the graph over(2/3)D, and
its centroid is0. Orient it toward the apex. Its cap is a pyramid of
volume8|D|/27, while its raw coarea section area is4|D|/9. Consequently

    p=(8/27)|D|/|B|,
    s=−|D|[1+9k·g_B]/(9|B|).                         (2)

Every vertical plane over a centered chord of B is centroidal too:
the section is the triangle formed by the apex and the two centered
base chord endpoints. Its centroid has height(2−1−1)/3=0 and
horizontal coordinate0. The cap fraction equals the planar cap
fraction for B. Its scalar correction term is(9/8) times the planar
one: the section-area ratio contributes3/2 and the centroid
projection contributes3/4. Again all these data are rational.

These are genuinely oblique central sections of nonsimplex convex
bodies. The construction uses exact centroids rather than numerical
normal roots. Bounded exact screenings using them have not supplied a
counterexample; this absence is not a proof of a scalar correction.
